newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada Reform pledges tax cuts, balanced budget.
newsitem.headline: Canada Reform pledges tax cuts, balanced budget.

text.p: Canada's right-wing Reform Party on Thursday kicked off its campaign for the expected 1997 federal election, pledging tax cuts, a balanced budget in about three years and more education and health care spending.

"These common sense policies reflect the concerns of Canadians and will go a long way to putting this country back on track," Reform leader Preston Manning told supporters in London, Ontario, about 180 km (113 miles) southwest of Toronto.
The populist Reform Party rallied conservative voters in western Canada to emerge from obscurity and become the third biggest party in parliament in the 1993 federal election.
It holds 51 seats in Canada's 295-seat House of Commons and in February narrowly lost a bid to replace the separatist Bloc Quebecois as Canada's official opposition.
The party's six-point plan was highlighted by a proposed government restructuring designed to save C$15 billion ($10.95 billion) a year and eliminate the deficit by March 31, 1999.

Canada's Liberal government seeks to cut the deficit to C$9 billion ($6.6 billion) by fiscal 1998/99 (April-March) and has said its goal is to balance the country's books. But Finance Minister Paul Martin has refused to set a date for bringing the deficit down to zero.

In a sharp reversal of Reform's previous plan to slash social programs, Manning promised to increase federal spending on health care and education by C$4 billion ($2.9 billion) a year, using some money he expects to save through the restructuring.

Manning also pledged to cut income taxes by C$2,000 ($1,460) a year for a family of four by the year 2000. The Liberal government opposes across-the-board tax cuts, but has not ruled out minor targeted tax cuts.
The Reform leader also promised a 28 percent cut in unemployment insurance premiums paid by employers and a 50 percent cut in capital gains taxes.
He said his goal was to "flatten" income taxes and replace the much reviled national sales tax (Goods and Services Tax), but stopped short of saying how Reform would finance its proposed tax cuts.
He also vowed a tough fight against crime, promising a binding referendum on the return of the death penalty.
As part of his strategy to keep Canada united, Manning promised decentralization and greater power to the provinces.
